item.title: Interpreting a Correlation Between Vehicle Weight and Fuel Economy
item.stimulus: An automotive magazine recorded, for each of 45 randomly selected new car models, the vehicle weight in pounds and the fuel economy in miles per gallon. Technology reports a correlation coefficient of r = −0.88 for these data.

parts.prompt: Interpret the value of r in context.

criteria.text: Interprets the sign of r = −0.88 as a negative association: as vehicle weight increases, fuel economy tends to decrease.
criteria.evidence: Response links the negative sign of r to the direction of the association in context.
criteria.fix: Read the sign of r as direction, then restate it in context using both variable names.

criteria.text: States that r = −0.88, which is close to -1, indicates a strong linear association between vehicle weight and fuel economy.
criteria.evidence: Response says the linear association is strong because r is close to -1, naming the two variables.
criteria.fix: Say how close r is to -1 or 1, call the linear association strong, moderate or weak, and name both variables.

parts.prompt: An editor says, "Because r = −0.88, a linear model is definitely appropriate for predicting fuel economy from vehicle weight." Explain why this reasoning is incomplete and what should be done before deciding that a linear model is appropriate.

criteria.text: States that a value of r as close to -1 or 1 as −0.88 does not by itself show that a linear model is appropriate.
criteria.evidence: Response says a correlation coefficient near -1 or 1 does not necessarily mean a linear model is appropriate.
criteria.fix: Remember r only measures linear association strength; a strong r can still come from a curved pattern, so r alone cannot justify a linear model.

criteria.text: States that a residual plot (or scatterplot) should be examined for curvature or other pattern before concluding a linear model is appropriate.
criteria.evidence: Response names a residual plot or a scatterplot as the check and says a pattern such as curvature would show the linear model is not appropriate.
criteria.fix: Name the check: make a residual plot and look for curvature; a random scatter supports a linear model.

parts.prompt: An editor also concludes that heavier vehicles cause lower fuel economy. Is this conclusion justified by the correlation? Explain.

criteria.text: States that correlation does not imply causation, so the association does not show that heavier vehicles cause lower fuel economy.
criteria.evidence: Response says an association or correlation, even a strong one, does not show that one variable causes changes in the other.
criteria.fix: Whenever a claim says one variable causes another, point out that a strong association does not establish causation.

parts.prompt: The analysts will also measure vehicle weight in different units, in kilograms instead of pounds. What value of r will they find for the new measurements? Explain.

criteria.text: States that r would still be −0.88 after measuring weight in kilograms instead of pounds because r is unit-free.
criteria.evidence: Response says r is unchanged and gives unit-free (not affected by the units of measurement) as the reason.
criteria.fix: Recall that r has no units, so changing the units of either variable by a positive-slope conversion leaves r unchanged.

item.model_answer:
(a) The correlation r = −0.88 is negative, so as vehicle weight increases, fuel economy tends to decrease. Because r is close to -1, the linear association between vehicle weight and fuel economy is strong.

(b) A value of r close to -1 or 1 does not necessarily mean a linear model is appropriate. The data could follow a curved pattern even when r is large. The analysts should look at a residual plot (or a scatterplot) and check for curvature or another pattern before deciding.

(c) No. Correlation does not imply causation. The strong association does not show that heavier vehicles cause lower fuel economy; other variables could account for the pattern.

(d) The new r will still be −0.88. The correlation coefficient is unit-free, so changing the units of measurement (measuring weight in kilograms instead of pounds) does not change r.
item.verification_python:
import math
def reg(x, y):
    n = len(x); mx = sum(x) / n; my = sum(y) / n
    sxx = sum((a - mx) ** 2 for a in x); syy = sum((b - my) ** 2 for b in y)
    sxy = sum((a - mx) * (b - my) for a, b in zip(x, y)); b = sxy / sxx
    return b, my - b * mx, sxy / math.sqrt(sxx * syy), mx, my
r = -0.88
assert -1 <= r <= 1 and abs(r) > 0.8
assert (r < 0) == True
xs = [2400, 2700, 3000, 3300, 3700, 4100, 4600]
ys = [39, 36, 34, 30, 27, 24, 21]
r1 = reg(xs, ys)[2]
r2 = reg([0.4536 * x for x in xs], ys)[2]
assert abs(r1 - r2) < 1e-12
print("ALL_CHECKS_PASSED")
